description: Decision patterns for encoding categorical variables

patterns.name: Low Cardinality Nominal
patterns.condition: Categorical column with <= 10 unique values AND no natural ordering
patterns.explanation: One-hot encoding creates binary columns for each category. Works best with low cardinality (≤10) to avoid dimensionality explosion. No ordering assumptions — pure nominal data.
patterns.pitfalls: Creates N new columns. Watch for multicollinearity in linear models (use drop_first=True).
patterns.business_impact: Preserves category independence. Essential for region, department, product_category analysis.
patterns.example: Applied one-hot encoding to 'region' (5 unique values: North, South, East, West, Central) — low cardinality, no natural order.

patterns.name: High Cardinality Nominal
patterns.condition: Categorical column with > 10 unique values AND no natural ordering
patterns.explanation: Frequency encoding replaces each category with its count (or proportion) in the dataset. Avoids dimensionality explosion from one-hot encoding high cardinality features.
patterns.pitfalls: Categories with similar frequencies become indistinguishable. Consider target encoding if a target variable is available.
patterns.business_impact: High cardinality one-hot encoding creates sparse matrices that slow down model training and increase memory by 10-50×.
patterns.example: Applied frequency encoding to 'zipcode' (2,847 unique values) — one-hot would create 2,847 new columns, causing memory issues.

patterns.name: Ordinal Categories
patterns.condition: Categorical column with natural ordering (e.g., Low < Medium < High)
patterns.explanation: Ordinal encoding assigns integers respecting the natural order (Low=1, Medium=2, High=3). Preserves the meaningful ranking relationship.
patterns.pitfalls: Assumes equal spacing between categories (Low→Medium = Medium→High). May need manual mapping definition.
patterns.business_impact: Preserves ranking information critical for customer tier analysis, satisfaction scoring, and priority-based operations.
patterns.example: Applied ordinal encoding to 'education_level': High School=1, Bachelor's=2, Master's=3, PhD=4 — natural academic progression.

patterns.name: Binary Categories
patterns.condition: Categorical column with exactly 2 unique values
patterns.explanation: Simple 0/1 encoding for binary features. No dimensionality increase, no ordering issues with just two values.
patterns.pitfalls: Ensure consistent mapping (e.g., Yes=1, No=0). Document which value maps to which.
patterns.business_impact: Clean binary representation for gender, yes/no, active/inactive features.
patterns.example: Applied label encoding to 'is_active': Active=1, Inactive=0 — binary column, straightforward mapping.

patterns.name: Target Encoding (Supervised)
patterns.condition: Categorical column with moderate-high cardinality AND target variable is available
patterns.explanation: Replaces each category with the mean of the target variable for that category. Captures the relationship between the category and the outcome.
patterns.pitfalls: HIGH RISK of target leakage. Must use proper cross-validation folds. Regularize with smoothing to prevent overfitting on rare categories.
patterns.business_impact: Powerful for prediction tasks but dangerous without proper implementation. Can inflate model performance artificially.
patterns.example: Applied smoothed target encoding to 'city' (156 unique values) with 5-fold cross-validation — mean target value per city captures geographic conversion patterns.

patterns.name: Text/Free-Form Categories
patterns.condition: Column contains free-form text entries with many slight variations
patterns.explanation: First standardize the text (lowercase, strip whitespace, fix typos), then group similar values, then apply appropriate encoding.
patterns.pitfalls: Skipping cleaning leads to artificially inflated cardinality (e.g., 'New York', 'new york', 'NY', 'newyork' counted as 4 categories).
patterns.business_impact: Uncleaned text categories fragment customer segments and product categories, reducing analysis accuracy by 20-40%.
patterns.example: Standardized 'city' column: merged 'New York'/'new york'/'NYC'/'NY' into 'New York' — reduced cardinality from 234 to 89 unique values.

decision_tree: 1. Is the column binary (2 unique values)? → Label encoding (0/1)
2. Does the column have natural ordering? → Ordinal encoding
4. Is cardinality high (> 10) AND target available? → Target encoding (with CV regularization)
5. Is cardinality high (> 10) AND no target? → Frequency encoding
6. Does the column have text/free-form variations? → Clean first, then re-evaluate cardinality
